task-waitasync-timeout-does-not-stop-ope.title: A Task.WaitAsync timeout does not stop the underlying operation
task-waitasync-timeout-does-not-stop-ope.short: Separate giving up on a wait from cancelling the work itself
task-waitasync-timeout-does-not-stop-ope.summary: Task.WaitAsync can stop waiting because of a timeout or cancellation while the original task continues unless its own operation is cancelled.
task-waitasync-timeout-does-not-stop-ope.why: Treating a timed-out wait as proof that the work stopped can leave I/O, mutations, or resource use running in the background.
task-waitasync-timeout-does-not-stop-ope.tips: Give the operation its own cancellation policy and explicitly decide whether a timeout should also request cancellation of that operation.

iasyncenumerable-enumerator-cancellation.title: Propagate enumeration cancellation through IAsyncEnumerable
iasyncenumerable-enumerator-cancellation.short: Connect WithCancellation to the iterator's actual work
iasyncenumerable-enumerator-cancellation.summary: Async iterators need to accept and use enumeration cancellation so callers can stop both iteration and the asynchronous operations behind it.
iasyncenumerable-enumerator-cancellation.why: A token supplied by the consumer is ineffective when the iterator ignores it or fails to combine it with its own cancellation parameter.
iasyncenumerable-enumerator-cancellation.tips: Use EnumeratorCancellation on the iterator token where appropriate and pass that token into every cancellable asynchronous operation in the loop.

pipewriter-flush-backpressure-boundary.title: Treat PipeWriter FlushAsync as a backpressure boundary
pipewriter-flush-backpressure-boundary.short: Advancing bytes is not the same as successfully flushing them downstream
pipewriter-flush-backpressure-boundary.summary: PipeWriter separates writing into acquired memory from flushing, allowing the pipeline to apply backpressure when buffered data grows.
pipewriter-flush-backpressure-boundary.why: Ignoring FlushAsync or producing without awaiting it can defeat flow control and increase buffered memory under a slow consumer.
pipewriter-flush-backpressure-boundary.tips: Advance only bytes actually written, await FlushAsync, and observe cancellation or completion results before continuing production.

assemblyloadcontext-plugin-type-identity.title: Preserve contract type identity across AssemblyLoadContext plugin boundaries
assemblyloadcontext-plugin-type-identity.short: Loading a second contract assembly creates different runtime types
assemblyloadcontext-plugin-type-identity.summary: AssemblyLoadContext enables isolated plugin loading, but type identity includes the assembly instance and loading context.
assemblyloadcontext-plugin-type-identity.why: A plugin can implement an interface with the same name and version yet fail casts when it loaded a separate copy of the contract assembly.
assemblyloadcontext-plugin-type-identity.tips: Define which assemblies are shared with the host, resolve them consistently, and isolate only dependencies that truly need separate loading.

filesystemwatcher-events-are-not-a-journ.title: Do not treat FileSystemWatcher events as a durable journal
filesystemwatcher-events-are-not-a-journ.short: File notifications can duplicate, reorder, or overflow
filesystemwatcher-events-are-not-a-journ.summary: FileSystemWatcher is useful for noticing possible filesystem changes, but its event stream is not an exactly-once history of all changes.
filesystemwatcher-events-are-not-a-journ.why: Applications that perform irreversible work once per event can duplicate work or miss state after buffer overflow and rapid filesystem activity.
filesystemwatcher-events-are-not-a-journ.tips: Debounce or queue notifications as hints, reconcile against durable filesystem/application state, and handle watcher overflow explicitly.

simd-vector-loop-tail-handling.title: Handle the scalar tail of SIMD loops explicitly
simd-vector-loop-tail-handling.short: Vector-width chunks rarely divide every input length exactly
simd-vector-loop-tail-handling.summary: SIMD loops process multiple elements per iteration, but inputs whose length is not a multiple of the vector width still need correct tail handling.
simd-vector-loop-tail-handling.why: A loop that assumes exact vector alignment can skip remaining elements or read beyond the valid span.
simd-vector-loop-tail-handling.tips: Process complete vectors while enough elements remain, then finish the residual elements with scalar code or a proven masked-vector strategy.

aspnetcore-response-caching-vary-boundar.title: Define safe variation boundaries for ASP.NET Core response caching
aspnetcore-response-caching-vary-boundar.short: Cache keys must include every request property that changes the representation
aspnetcore-response-caching-vary-boundar.summary: Response caching is safe only when reusable responses and their variation dimensions match the application's authentication and content rules.
aspnetcore-response-caching-vary-boundar.why: Caching a response that varies by user, header, query value, or authorization state without reflecting that boundary can serve the wrong representation.
aspnetcore-response-caching-vary-boundar.tips: Cache only explicitly reusable responses and configure variation rules around the request data that actually changes response content.

unity-burst-managed-object-boundary.title: Keep managed objects outside Unity Burst job data
unity-burst-managed-object-boundary.short: Burst-compiled jobs work best with blittable and native data
unity-burst-managed-object-boundary.summary: Burst optimizes a constrained subset of .NET code and job data, while ordinary managed object graphs and runtime services remain outside that boundary.
unity-burst-managed-object-boundary.why: Capturing managed references or relying on unsupported managed behavior prevents Burst compilation or forces architecture that cannot run inside jobs.
unity-burst-managed-object-boundary.tips: Prepare data before scheduling, store job inputs in supported value/native containers, and move managed-object interaction back to non-Burst code.

json-utf8reader-ref-struct-lifetime.title: Respect Utf8JsonReader ref-struct and buffer lifetime boundaries
json-utf8reader-ref-struct-lifetime.short: The reader is a transient cursor over caller-owned UTF-8 data
json-utf8reader-ref-struct-lifetime.summary: Utf8JsonReader is a ref struct designed for allocation-conscious token parsing over spans or sequences with explicit reader state.
json-utf8reader-ref-struct-lifetime.why: Trying to retain the reader across unsupported async boundaries or outlive its backing data conflicts with its stack-oriented lifetime model.
json-utf8reader-ref-struct-lifetime.tips: Consume tokens within the valid buffer lifetime and preserve JsonReaderState rather than the reader itself when incremental parsing crosses buffer boundaries.

concurrentdictionary-value-factory-may-r.title: ConcurrentDictionary value factories may execute more than once
concurrentdictionary-value-factory-may-r.short: Atomic insertion does not imply single execution of expensive factories
concurrentdictionary-value-factory-may-r.summary: ConcurrentDictionary can invoke competing value factories concurrently even though only one resulting value is stored for a key.
concurrentdictionary-value-factory-may-r.why: Factories with side effects or expensive resource creation can run multiple times under contention and leak or duplicate work.
concurrentdictionary-value-factory-may-r.tips: Keep factories cheap and side-effect free, or store a Lazy/Task-like single-flight value when creation itself must be coordinated.
